query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of titanium to the CoCrFeNi high‐entropy‐alloy matrix will enable the in situ formation of a stable, low-shear oxide tribofilm over the entire sliding temperature range, thereby ensuring low coefficient of friction and reduced wear even at 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: Baseline equiatomic CoCrFeNi alloy that exhibits low friction at room temperature but suffers from increased friction and wear at elevated temperatures due to uncontrolled oxide formation and tribochemical reactions.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor titanium alloying addition (on the order of 1 at% or similar) into the CoCrFeNi composition.
generation.conditions: Dry sliding wear tests conducted in ambient air with temperatures ranging from room temperature (≈25 °C) up to 800 °C under consistent load and sliding speed conditions similar to those used in prior studies.
generation.structural_mediator: The titanium addition is expected to promote the preferential formation of a finely dispersed, adherent oxide phase (e.g., a mixed Ti-containing spinel or rutile/TiO2 phase) that acts as a lubricious tribofilm at high temperatures while preserving the solid-solution microstructure at low temperatures.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, titanium oxidizes more readily than the parent elements, leading to the controlled in situ formation of a continuous, protective oxide layer that effectively reduces friction and wear by providing a low-shear interface. At lower temperatures, the small titanium content does not significantly disrupt the alloy’s favorable solid-solution properties, maintaining low friction.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified CoCrFeNi alloy, the titanium-modified alloy should exhibit a consistently lower coefficient of friction and reduced wear rate across the entire test temperature range, with the most significant improvements observed at high temperatures (e.g., 800 °C) where oxide-mediated tribological degradation normally occurs.
generation.baseline: CoCrFeNi alloy that shows low friction at room temperature but experiences increased friction and higher wear rates at elevated temperatures due to uncontrolled oxide formation and tribochemical reactions.
generation.boundary: Performance is expected under dry sliding conditions in ambient atmosphere with temperatures from ~25 °C to 800 °C and under the same mechanical load and sliding speed conditions as those used in prior sliding wear studies.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal titanium concentration and the detailed nature (phase, morphology, thickness) of the oxide tribofilm are not precisely known. There is also uncertainty regarding possible impacts on the bulk mechanical properties which will need verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of samples: one with the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy and one with an identical alloy doped with a minor (~1 at%) amount of titanium. Conduct dry sliding wear tests at multiple temperatures (e.g., 25 °C, 400 °C, and 800 °C) under identical loading and sliding speeds. Post-test, characterize the wear tracks using SEM, EDS, and XRD to evaluate oxide formation and morphology.
measurements: Coefficient of friction (COF) vs. sliding distance/time at each test temperature
Wear volume or track depth measurements
Identification and characterization of surface oxide phases via XRD/EDS analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the titanium-doped samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in COF and worn volume (or wear rate) compared to the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy at high temperature (and no evidence of a controlled, adherent oxide tribofilm is found), then the hypothesis is falsified.

System: AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Inert gas atomisation using argon followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1050 °C for 10 min under 50 MPa compaction pressure, with passive cooling at 150 K/min until 300 °C.
